notes.summary: In Sentence Improvement a part of the sentence is underlined or bold. You choose the option that corrects it, or 'No improvement' if it is already correct. The tested rules are the same as error spotting, but here you must also pick the right fix.

concepts.title: Check the underlined part only
concepts.body: The rest of the sentence is correct and gives you clues (tense, number, subject). Your answer must fit smoothly into it. Read the full sentence with each option in place.

concepts.title: Common areas
concepts.body:
• Conditionals: If I were you, I would…; If he had studied, he would have passed.
  • Tense sequence: a past main verb usually takes a past verb in the reported clause.
  • Redundancy: return back, repeat again, cousin brother are wrong.
  • Idiomatic forms: look forward to meeting, used to living (when 'used to' means accustomed).

concepts.title: 'No improvement' is a real option
concepts.body: If the underlined part is grammatically correct and natural, choose 'No improvement'. Do not change a correct sentence just because another option also sounds fine.

varieties.name: Conditionals and tense
varieties.how: Match the if-clause with the main clause: present–will, past–would, past perfect–would have.

example.q: If she would have left early, she would have caught the train.
steps: Main clause is would have caught (type 3, unreal past).
The if-clause needs past perfect: had left.

varieties.name: Redundancy and idiom
varieties.how: Remove words that repeat a meaning already present, and use the fixed English form.

example.q: Please return back the book by Monday.

varieties.name: Spotting a correct sentence
varieties.how: Check subject, verb, tense, preposition. If all are right, choose 'No improvement'.

steps: since + a point in time with present perfect continuous is correct.

tips: Eliminate options that introduce a new error; usually two options can be dropped quickly.
After look forward to, object to, be used to, with a view to, the verb takes -ing.
traps: Would never goes in the if-clause of a conditional.
Used to + verb (past habit) and be used to + -ing (accustomed) mean different things.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to improve the bold part.
The teacher asked the boy to repeat again his answer.
questions.solution: Repeat already means 'say again', so again is redundant. Correct: repeat his answer.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to improve the bold part.
She has been living in Pune for ten years.
questions.solution: for ten years describes an action that started in the past and continues now, so the present perfect continuous has been living is correct. No improvement.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to improve the bold part.
If I was the Prime Minister, I would build more schools.
questions.solution: For an imaginary present situation, English uses the subjunctive were for all persons: If I were…, I would…

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to improve the bold part.
We are looking forward to meet you at the conference.
questions.solution: In look forward to, to is a preposition, so it takes a gerund: looking forward to meeting.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to improve the bold part.
Had he listened to his doctor, he will not fall ill.
questions.solution: Had he listened = If he had listened (type 3, unreal past). The main clause must be would not have fallen.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to improve the bold part.
Hardly had we reached the station when the train left.
questions.solution: With a negative adverb like Hardly at the start, the auxiliary comes before the subject: Hardly had we reached … when. The sentence is already correct.

flashcards.back: If + had + V3, … would have + V3
look forward to meeting — 'to' is a preposition here
